claims.text: An ultrathin Cr-based interlayer enhances interface coherency in HEA multilayer coatings.
Enhancing interface coherency with a Cr-based interlayer shifts the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
HEA multilayers without a transition layer exhibit mixed creep behavior dominated by diffusion at elevated temperatures.
High-temperature creep tests under controlled mechanical loading replicate service conditions typical of advanced coating applications.
A Cr-based interlayer promotes lattice coherency at interfaces between HEA layers.
An ultrathin Cr interlayer reduces lattice mismatch in an HEA multilayer.
Reducing lattice mismatch with a Cr interlayer can lower diffusion barriers.
A Cr interlayer modulates dislocation-nucleation sites.
Controlled adjustment of the interfacial structure reduces diffusion-creep tendencies.
Controlled adjustment of the interfacial structure enables a transition to dislocation-mediated creep.
Cr-modified HEA multilayers will have lower diffusion-controlled creep rates than multilayers without the interlayer.
Cr-modified HEA multilayers will exhibit greater dislocation activity and dislocation density than control multilayers.
Diffusion-mediated creep predominates at high temperatures in HEA multilayers lacking a Cr-based interlayer.
The proposed creep-mechanism transition requires an optimal ultrathin Cr-interlayer thickness.
An excessively thick Cr-based layer could cause brittle-phase formation.
An excessively thick Cr-based layer could cause adverse microstructural changes.
The critical Cr-interlayer thickness and quantitative magnitude of the creep-mechanism shift remain undetermined.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says that the Cr interlayer lowers diffusion barriers, which would ordinarily facilitate diffusion, while also claiming that the same change reduces diffusion-creep tendencies and diffusion-controlled creep rates. No additional explanation resolves this internally opposing direction.
